objective: Investigate the dual-write problem, Transactional Outbox pattern, polling publisher with SKIP LOCKED, log-based CDC with Debezium, replication slot safeguards, and consumer Inbox deduplication.

key_findings: Dual-write operations between databases and message brokers are formally impossible without 2PC; the Transactional Outbox pattern guarantees atomicity by staging events in local ACID transactions.
Log-based Change Data Capture (CDC) via Debezium streaming from PostgreSQL WAL (pgoutput) achieves 80,000 events/sec with sub-35ms latency and zero database query overhead.
Replication slots without max_slot_wal_keep_size limits risk 100% disk exhaustion during consumer outages; configuring a 50GB retention cap protects core database availability.
Kafka partition keys must strictly match domain aggregate IDs (e.g. order_id) to guarantee total FIFO ordering per entity across distributed broker clusters.
The Inbox Pattern with relational UNIQUE(event_id) constraints provides foolproof consumer idempotency, neutralizing duplicate message deliveries under at-least-once brokers.
inferences: [INFERENCE] Log-based CDC pipelines will entirely displace polling publishers in modern microservices, operating as transparent infrastructure managed by platform teams.
[INFERENCE] PostgreSQL 17 synchronized failover replication slots will make zero-data-loss CDC pipelines the default standard across high-availability multi-AZ architectures.
critical_gaps: Failing to configure max_slot_wal_keep_size can cause crashed CDC consumers to fill the database disk with retained WAL segments, halting the entire company.
Unpartitioned outbox tables subject to frequent DELETE statements suffer massive PostgreSQL MVCC vacuum bloat; daily range partitioning with DROP TABLE is required.

rounds.topic: The Formal Impossibility of Distributed Dual-Write without 2PC
rounds.finding: Writing to an ACID database and a message broker sequentially cannot guarantee atomicity under partial network partitions. If the broker write fails post-commit, events are lost; if the DB rolls back post-publish, phantom events corrupt state.

rounds.topic: Failure Modes of Write-to-DB-then-Publish-to-Kafka
rounds.finding: When the application commits to PostgreSQL and crashes before publishing to Kafka, the business state is updated, but downstream microservices (billing, inventory, shipping) never receive the event, resulting in silent data drift.

rounds.topic: Failure Modes of Publish-to-Kafka-then-Write-to-DB
rounds.finding: If the application publishes to Kafka first and the database transaction aborts (e.g., unique constraint violation), downstream consumers act on an order that never formally existed in the system.

rounds.topic: Two-Phase Commit (2PC / XA) Performance Bottlenecks
rounds.finding: Traditional XA/2PC protocols coordinate atomicity across heterogeneous resources but hold database locks across two network round-trips, collapsing transaction throughput from 25,000 TPS to under 400 TPS.

rounds.topic: Event-Driven Consistency and BASE Semantics
rounds.finding: Modern microservice architectures abandon distributed 2PC in favor of BASE (Basically Available, Soft-state, Eventual consistency), relying on reliable event delivery to converge system state.

rounds.topic: The Role of At-Least-Once Delivery Guarantees
rounds.finding: Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redpanda) guarantee at-least-once delivery; downstream systems must expect and tolerate duplicate event delivery through idempotent consumer design.

rounds.topic: Local Transaction Boundary as the Root of Trust
rounds.finding: By restricting atomic operations strictly to the local relational database transaction, systems achieve 100% durability and atomicity at full wire speed without external distributed consensus.

rounds.topic: Impact of Network Jitter and Asynchronous TCP Timeouts
rounds.finding: Transient network partitions between application pods and Kafka brokers produce false-negative timeouts where messages are published but ACK is lost, forcing retry amplification.

rounds.topic: Auditability and Regulatory Requirements for Business Events
rounds.finding: Financial regulations (SOX, PCI-DSS) mandate that every ledger mutation produces an immutable, ordered audit log event; losing events due to dual-write failures incurs severe regulatory penalties.

rounds.topic: Architectural Synthesis: Why the Transactional Outbox Is Non-Negotiable
rounds.finding: The Transactional Outbox pattern is the industry standard architectural solution, bridging the gap between local relational transactions and distributed asynchronous messaging.

rounds.topic: Outbox Table Schema Design and Required Metadata
rounds.finding: The outbox table schema requires: id (UUID/BIGINT), aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload (JSONB), created_at (TIMESTAMP), and headers (JSONB tracing metadata).

rounds.topic: Atomic Staging inside the Business Transaction
rounds.finding: Within a single BEGIN ... COMMIT block, the application inserts or updates the business domain entity (e.g. orders) and inserts the corresponding event row into the outbox table.

rounds.topic: Decoupling Domain Mutation from Network I/O
rounds.finding: By staging events in the outbox table, the critical path of the user HTTP request completes with zero dependency on message broker latency, network partitions, or broker maintenance windows.

rounds.topic: Payload Serialization: Protobuf vs Avro vs JSONB
rounds.finding: Storing payloads as JSONB allows native SQL querying and debugging, whereas binary Protobuf or Avro reduces outbox table storage footprint by 65% and accelerates serialization.

rounds.topic: Multi-Tenant Outbox Isolation Strategies
rounds.finding: Multi-tenant architectures partition outbox tables by tenant_id or co-locate tenant outbox rows on matching database shards to maintain tenant data sovereignty and isolation.

rounds.topic: Distributed Tracing Context Propagation in Outbox Headers
rounds.finding: Serializing W3C Trace Context (traceparent, tracestate) into the outbox headers column preserves end-to-end distributed tracing spans from user request through asynchronous Kafka consumers.

rounds.topic: Event Versioning and Schema Evolution Handling
rounds.finding: Including an event_version integer in the outbox schema supports forward and backward compatibility (e.g. adding non-breaking optional fields) as domain event structures evolve.

rounds.topic: Handling High-Frequency Updates on the Same Aggregate
rounds.finding: When an aggregate mutates multiple times per second, emitting discrete fine-grained events preserves complete state history, while state-snapshot events reduce event bus volume.

rounds.topic: Outbox Write Overhead on Relational Database IOPS
rounds.finding: Inserting an outbox record in the same transaction increases write IOPS by ~15-20% (an extra row insert and WAL logging), easily absorbed by modern NVMe SSD storage.

rounds.topic: Comparative Evaluation: In-DB Outbox vs Event Sourcing
rounds.finding: Full Event Sourcing treats the event log as the source of truth; Transactional Outbox provides identical event streaming benefits while allowing teams to retain familiar relational tables.

rounds.topic: Polling Publisher Architecture and Draining Loop
rounds.finding: A dedicated background publisher service periodically queries the outbox table (e.g. every 200ms), retrieves pending events, publishes them to Kafka, and marks them processed.

rounds.topic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Mechanics in PostgreSQL
rounds.finding: Using SKIP LOCKED allows multiple concurrent publisher workers to acquire non-overlapping batches of uncommitted rows without blocking each other or waiting on row locks.

rounds.topic: Polling Lag vs Database CPU Churn Trade-off
rounds.finding: Frequent polling (e.g. 50ms) achieves low latency but consumes 30-40% database CPU running empty queries during quiet periods; long polling intervals increase end-to-end event latency.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY for Event-Driven Polling Wakeup
rounds.finding: Triggering pg_notify('outbox_channel', 'new_event') upon outbox insert awakens the polling publisher immediately, providing sub-10ms delivery without continuous CPU polling churn.

rounds.topic: Batch Size Sizing and Network Pipeline Optimization
rounds.finding: Fetching events in batches of 500 to 1,000 records optimizes database query execution and allows batch publishing to Kafka, achieving 25,000 events/sec publisher throughput.

rounds.topic: Publisher Failure Recovery and Transaction Boundaries
rounds.finding: The publisher must mark outbox records as sent ONLY after receiving synchronous ACK from Kafka; if the publisher crashes mid-batch, rows are safely re-processed on restart.

rounds.topic: Worker Scalability and Partition Assignment
rounds.finding: Scaling polling publishers across multiple Kubernetes pods requires assigning workers to distinct outbox partitions (e.g. WHERE id % N = worker_id) to avoid redundant lock checking.

rounds.topic: Outbox Table Deletion Strategies (DELETE vs UPDATE status)
rounds.finding: Updating status = 'PROCESSED' bloats table indexes; immediately deleting processed rows (DELETE) keeps the table tiny (<1,000 rows), but creates PostgreSQL MVCC dead tuple churn.

rounds.topic: Handling Poison Pill Events in Polling Publishers
rounds.finding: If a corrupted event payload fails Kafka publishing repeatedly, the publisher moves the row to an outbox_dead_letter table after 5 retries to prevent queue head-of-line blocking.

rounds.topic: Limitations of Polling Publishers at Extreme Scale
rounds.finding: Beyond 50,000 events/sec, polling publishers saturate relational database query capacity; architectures must transition to log-based Change Data Capture (CDC).

rounds.topic: Log-Based CDC Architecture: Reading the Write-Ahead Log
rounds.finding: Log-based Change Data Capture intercepts commits directly from PostgreSQL Write-Ahead Log (WAL) or MySQL binary log, bypassing SQL query execution completely.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL Logical Decoding and pgoutput Plugin Internals
rounds.finding: PostgreSQL logical decoding extracts committed row mutations from WAL. The built-in pgoutput plugin streams logical change records (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) to subscribers.

rounds.topic: Debezium Outbox Event Router SMT (Single Message Transform)
rounds.finding: Debezium includes a native Outbox Event Router transform that intercepts inserts into the outbox table, strips CDC metadata, and routes the pure domain payload directly to Kafka topics.

rounds.topic: Dynamic Topic Routing via Event Type Metadata
rounds.finding: The Debezium outbox router dynamically sets destination Kafka topics using the outbox event_type column (e.g. order.created -> topic: order-events), enabling flexible routing.

rounds.topic: Zero Database Query Overhead under CDC Streaming
rounds.finding: Because CDC reads sequential WAL log files directly from disk or memory buffers, it exerts near-zero CPU and query lock overhead on active database transactions.

rounds.topic: Debezium Connector High Availability and Offset Management
rounds.finding: Debezium records its consumed Log Sequence Number (LSN) in an internal Kafka topic (connect-offsets), allowing seamless failover across Kafka Connect worker nodes.

rounds.topic: Snapshot Mode vs Streaming Mode Lifecycle
rounds.finding: When initializing a new CDC connector, Debezium performs a consistent initial snapshot of the outbox table before seamlessly transitioning to real-time WAL streaming.

rounds.topic: Network Throughput Scaling: Sustaining 80,000 Events/sec
rounds.finding: Under continuous load benchmarks, a single Debezium Kafka Connect task streams 80,000 events/sec from PostgreSQL WAL into Kafka with sub-35ms propagation latency.

rounds.topic: Debezium Engine Embedded Mode in Go and Java
rounds.finding: Teams avoiding heavy Kafka Connect infrastructure run Debezium Embedded inside lightweight Go/Java worker daemons, reading WAL directly and pushing to NATS JetStream or Kafka.

rounds.topic: Comparative Matrix: Polling Publisher vs Debezium CDC
rounds.finding: Polling Publisher is simpler to set up but consumes DB CPU and caps at ~15k QPS; Debezium CDC requires replication permissions and slot management but scales to 100k+ QPS with zero DB CPU churn.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL Replication Slots and WAL Retention Mechanics
rounds.finding: A replication slot instructs PostgreSQL to preserve all WAL files generated since the slot's last acknowledged LSN, preventing WAL pruning before consumers process changes.

rounds.topic: The Stalled Consumer Disaster: Infinite WAL Accumulation
rounds.finding: If Debezium crashes or Kafka Connect stops processing, PostgreSQL retains 100% of generated WAL files indefinitely, rapidly filling disk storage and halting the primary database.

rounds.topic: pg_replication_slots View and Replication Lag Metrics
rounds.finding: Monitoring pg_replication_slots queries active, confirmed_flush_lsn, and pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn) to detect consumer lag in real time.

rounds.topic: Configuring max_slot_wal_keep_size as the Ultimate Circuit Breaker
rounds.finding: Setting max_slot_wal_keep_size (e.g. 50GB) limits the maximum WAL retained by replication slots. If consumer lag exceeds 50GB, the slot is invalidated, saving the database from disk crash.

rounds.topic: Re-Snapshotting Runbook when Replication Slots Invalidate
rounds.finding: When max_slot_wal_keep_size drops an invalid slot, Debezium triggers an error. Operators must re-create the slot and execute an incremental snapshot to restore event continuity.

rounds.topic: WAL Disk Space Sizing and Auto-Expanding Cloud Volumes
rounds.finding: Sizing database storage with at least 3x the peak daily WAL generation volume (e.g. 500GB volume for 150GB daily WAL) provides sufficient buffer for multi-hour consumer outages.

rounds.topic: Prometheus Alerting Rules for Replication Slot Lag
rounds.finding: Alerting rules fire when replication lag exceeds 5GB for >10 minutes (Warning) or 20GB for >5 minutes (Critical), enabling automated PagerDuty dispatch before disk saturation.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL 17 Logical Replication Failover Slots
rounds.finding: PostgreSQL 17 introduces synchronized logical replication slots between primary and standby replicas, allowing Debezium to fail over to replica databases without missing events.

rounds.topic: Vacuuming Impact on Long-Running Logical Transactions
rounds.finding: Uncommitted transactions in PostgreSQL block VACUUM cleanup across the entire database. Ensuring outbox transactions commit rapidly prevents global transaction ID wraparound risks.

rounds.topic: Production Checklist: Hardening CDC Replication Slots
rounds.finding: Enterprise deployment guidelines mandating max_slot_wal_keep_size, 24/7 LSN lag telemetry, dedicated monitoring daemons, and automated slot drop alerts.

rounds.topic: Kafka Partition Total Ordering Guarantees
rounds.finding: Kafka guarantees strict FIFO total message ordering within an individual topic partition. Total ordering across multiple partitions is physically impossible in distributed brokers.

rounds.topic: Selecting the Optimal Kafka Partition Key
rounds.finding: Using the business aggregate ID (e.g. order_id or account_id) as the Kafka record key ensures all events for that specific entity land on the exact same partition in sequence.

rounds.topic: Hotspot Partitioning Skew and High-Volume Tenants
rounds.finding: If a single tenant generates 100x more traffic than others, routing purely on tenant_id overloads a single partition. Composite keys (tenant_id:order_id) distribute load evenly.

rounds.topic: Producer Retries and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection
rounds.finding: If producer retries occur while multiple in-flight batches are in transit, batch 2 could succeed before retried batch 1, causing out-of-order writes; enable.idempotence=true eliminates this.

rounds.topic: Kafka Idempotent Producer Semantics (enable.idempotence)
rounds.finding: Setting enable.idempotence=true assigns a Producer ID (PID) and sequence number to every batch. The broker rejects duplicate sequence numbers, guaranteeing exactly-once publish to partition.

rounds.topic: Consumer Group Rebalancing and Partition Reassignment
rounds.finding: When consumer pods scale up or crash, Kafka rebalances partitions. CooperativeStickyAssignor minimizes partition movements, preserving event stream continuity during deploys.

rounds.topic: Handling Poison Pill Events in Kafka Partitions
rounds.finding: If a single corrupted event crashes consumer pods, the partition stalls. Consumers must catch serialization exceptions, write the event to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ), and commit the offset.

rounds.topic: End-to-End Latency: From Outbox Commit to Consumer Processing
rounds.finding: Measuring P99 latency from outbox row insert to consumer processing: Debezium CDC achieves 32ms P99; polling publisher achieves 280ms P99 under 50k events/sec.

rounds.topic: Kafka Log Compaction for State-Snapshot Topics
rounds.finding: Configuring cleanup.policy=compact on entity snapshot topics retains only the latest state for each primary key, providing instant entity hydration for new microservice instances.

rounds.topic: Production Throughput Scaling: Partition Count Sizing
rounds.finding: Sizing Kafka topics with 64 to 128 partitions sustains over 250,000 events/sec throughput while providing granular concurrency across consumer worker pods.

rounds.topic: The Necessity of Idempotent Consumers under At-Least-Once Delivery
rounds.finding: Because Kafka and CDC pipelines guarantee at-least-once delivery, network retries or consumer restarts inevitably deliver duplicate events; consumers must enforce idempotency.

rounds.topic: The Inbox Pattern Architecture
rounds.finding: The Inbox Pattern mirrors the Outbox pattern on the receiving end: incoming events are recorded in an inbox table within the target business transaction to prevent duplicate processing.

rounds.topic: Atomic Deduplication Table Constraint (UNIQUE event_id)
rounds.finding: Inserting the event UUID into an inbox table with a UNIQUE(event_id) constraint inside the business transaction guarantees that duplicate deliveries fail with an ignorable constraint error.

rounds.topic: Redis Atomic Key Deduplication (SETNX) for Fast Path
rounds.finding: For high-throughput non-relational services, checking Redis via SET event:1001 1 NX EX 86400 provides sub-millisecond deduplication with automatic 24-hour expiration.

rounds.topic: Race Conditions in Read-then-Insert Deduplication Checks
rounds.finding: Querying SELECT count(*) FROM inbox WHERE event_id = ? before inserting introduces a race condition under concurrent duplicate deliveries; using INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is mandatory.

rounds.topic: Handling Idempotent Side Effects: External Third-Party APIs
rounds.finding: When consumer processing invokes non-idempotent third-party APIs (e.g. Stripe charge), the consumer must persist a local intent state before external execution to enable reconciliation.

rounds.topic: Inbox Table Sizing and Asynchronous Pruning
rounds.finding: Like outbox tables, inbox tables accumulate millions of processed event IDs. Daily partition dropping or background pruning of records older than 7 days prevents table bloat.

rounds.topic: Consumer Error Handling: Retrying Transient vs Fatal Errors
rounds.finding: Database deadlocks or network timeouts are retried with exponential backoff; schema validation errors or business rule rejections are logged to DLQ and acknowledged immediately.

rounds.topic: Performance Overhead of Inbox Deduplication Inserts
rounds.finding: Inserting an inbox record within the consumer transaction adds ~1.2ms latency, a minor trade-off that completely eliminates double-billing and duplicate order creation.

rounds.topic: Production Implementation: Go Idempotent Consumer Middleware
rounds.finding: Wrapping consumer handler functions in a reusable Go middleware that executes deduplication inserts, transaction commit, and Kafka offset acknowledgement.

rounds.topic: The Out-of-Order Event Challenge across Network Boundaries
rounds.finding: Even with partition ordering, consumer restarts, parallel processing threads, or network re-routing can cause consumers to receive Event Version 3 before Event Version 2.

rounds.topic: Monotonic Version Numbers in Aggregate Roots
rounds.finding: Every domain aggregate maintains an integer version column incremented with each mutation (e.g. Order version=1, 2, 3). Events carry this aggregate version as metadata.

rounds.topic: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) Consumer Validation
rounds.finding: Consumers validate incoming event versions against local state: if event.version == local.version + 1, update is applied; if event.version <= local.version, event is a duplicate.

rounds.topic: Buffer-and-Wait Pattern for Out-of-Order Sequences
rounds.finding: If an incoming event version is ahead of local state (event.version > local.version + 1), the consumer buffers the event in Redis or a staging table and waits for missing events.

rounds.topic: Gap Detection and Active Re-synchronization Requests
rounds.finding: If a version gap persists beyond a timeout window (e.g. 5 seconds), the consumer queries the source service API directly to fetch the current aggregate snapshot and bridge the gap.

rounds.topic: Event Sourcing Replay and Projection Reconstruction
rounds.finding: For read-model projection databases, replaying events in strict sequence order reconstructs exact state, resolving any inconsistencies caused by temporary out-of-order processing.

rounds.topic: Vector Clocks vs Lamport Timestamps in Distributed Sagas
rounds.finding: When events span multiple collaborating microservices without a single aggregate root, Lamport timestamps or vector clocks establish partial causal ordering across events.

rounds.topic: Idempotent State Replacement (Last-Write-Wins Pitfalls)
rounds.finding: Applying full state replacement without version checks allows delayed older events to overwrite newer data; version-checked atomic updates (WHERE version < new_version) prevent regression.

rounds.topic: Telemetry: Tracking Out-of-Order Rates in Production
rounds.finding: Exposing metrics tracking event_sequence_gap_total and event_buffer_wait_duration_ms identifies misconfigured partition keys or consumer concurrency bugs.

rounds.topic: Production Validation: 100k Out-of-Order Simulation Benchmark
rounds.finding: Injecting 10% out-of-order events into a 100k event stream: buffer-and-wait reconciliation restored 100% data consistency without operator intervention.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL MVCC Dead Tuple Generation from High-Volume Inserts/Deletes
rounds.finding: Executing 50,000 INSERT and DELETE operations/sec on an unpartitioned outbox table generates billions of dead tuples daily, overwhelming PostgreSQL autovacuum.

rounds.topic: Table Bloat and Index Degradation Mechanics
rounds.finding: Vacuum cannot reclaim disk space back to the OS, causing the outbox table and its indexes to expand to hundreds of gigabytes, degrading query and insert performance.

rounds.topic: Range Partitioning by Date / Time (PARTITION BY RANGE)
rounds.finding: Partitioning the outbox table by day or hour (PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)) groups events into isolated physical table files.

rounds.topic: Instantaneous Partition Dropping via DROP TABLE
rounds.finding: Instead of running expensive DELETE queries, the cleanup worker executes DROP TABLE outbox_2026_09_10. Dropping a partition takes <2ms, deletes zero WAL dead tuples, and frees disk to OS.

rounds.topic: pg_partman: Automated Partition Lifecycle Management
rounds.finding: Using the pg_partman extension automates future partition creation and drops expired partitions automatically according to configured data retention policies.

rounds.topic: Co-locating Outbox Partitions on Sharded Databases (Vitess/Citus)
rounds.finding: In horizontally sharded databases, outbox table partitions must be co-located with business entity tables using the exact same shard distribution key to ensure local transaction atomicity.

rounds.topic: Optimizing Autovacuum Parameters for High-Turnover Tables
rounds.finding: For unpartitioned legacy outbox tables, tuning autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.01 and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit=2000 prevents autovacuum from falling hopelessly behind.

rounds.topic: TRUNCATE vs DELETE Performance and Lock Escalation
rounds.finding: TRUNCATE acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table, blocking all concurrent transactions; scheduled partition drops avoid table-wide locks.

rounds.topic: Monitoring Table Bloat via pgstattuple and pg_stat_user_tables
rounds.finding: Querying n_dead_tup and pgstattuple dead tuple percentages provides real-time alerts when table bloat exceeds 20% of total table volume.

rounds.topic: Production Runbook: Zero-Bloat Outbox Table Maintenance
rounds.finding: Standard operating procedure mandating daily range partitioning, pre-creation of 7-day future partitions, and automated dropping of partitions older than 48 hours.

rounds.topic: PostgreSQL 100% Disk Outage from Crashed Debezium Connector
rounds.finding: A Debezium pod encountered a fatal out-of-memory crash over a holiday weekend. Over 48 hours, PostgreSQL retained 380GB of WAL files, filling the 500GB volume and halting the database.

rounds.topic: Root Cause: Absence of max_slot_wal_keep_size Safeguard
rounds.finding: The database was deployed with default max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1 (unlimited). The replication slot forced PostgreSQL to retain all WAL files rather than dropping the slot.

rounds.topic: Emergency Recovery Procedure: Dropping the Replication Slot
rounds.finding: Database administrators executed SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_slot') to instantly free 380GB of WAL files, bringing the primary database back online.

rounds.topic: Post-Mortem Remediation: Enforcing max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB
rounds.finding: Configured max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB across all production clusters, guaranteeing replication slots will drop before disk consumption reaches 80%.

rounds.topic: Duplicate Payment Charges from Missing Consumer Idempotency
rounds.finding: A network glitch caused Kafka to re-deliver a batch of 1,200 payment events. Downstream consumer lacked an inbox deduplication table, charging customer credit cards twice.

rounds.topic: Remediation: Deploying the Inbox Pattern with Unique Key Constraints
rounds.finding: Integrated the Inbox pattern with a relational UNIQUE(event_id) constraint in the payment database, ensuring 100% of duplicate event deliveries are safely ignored.

rounds.topic: Outbox Table Vacuum Bloat Freezing Database Storage
rounds.finding: A polling publisher running continuous DELETE queries generated 45GB of dead tuples, causing query plans to switch to sequential table scans and degrading query latency by 12x.

rounds.topic: Remediation: Migrating to Daily Range Partitioning with DROP TABLE
rounds.finding: Re-architected the outbox table to use pg_partman daily range partitioning, replacing DELETE queries with instantaneous partition drops and eliminating table bloat.

rounds.topic: Kafka Broker Split-Brain Causing Out-of-Order Events
rounds.finding: A ZooKeeper network split caused Kafka partition leadership flapping, delivering order events out of sequence and creating ghost items in shipping inventories.

rounds.topic: Production Architecture Standard: 2027 Resilient Outbox Ecosystem
rounds.finding: Consolidated master specification: PostgreSQL 17 logical replication, Debezium CDC with Outbox Event Router, max_slot_wal_keep_size=50GB, and Consumer Inbox deduplication.
